Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00749

This does not conflict with existence being first among all things that come from a cause. The discussion here looks at the essence in relation to its existence and to the cause that gives it existence. Something may also come later in its dependent existence than something that is prior to it in itself. For example, in natural philosophy, one establishes that motion exists before proving that it has a source and an unmoved mover whose power has no limit. The body’s changing nature is considered first; only later is it shown to have a mover that is necessary in itself, even though that Necessary Being is prior to all things in reality. So there is no contradiction in existence being prior to essence in itself, while the mind considers essence and its earlier conditions first as it traces their dependence on existence.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00750
1. A point to keep in mind
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00751

We have hinted at this and will explain it further. A general idea in the mind, whether it describes what a thing is or a feature it has, is not what the One who exists through Himself brings into being. What is directly caused is existence itself, whether that existence is called originated or enduring. In fact, if both depend on another, enduring existence depends on its cause even more than originated existence does.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00752

When you analyze originated existence into the fact that something was absent and then became present, you see that its prior nonexistence is not directly caused by an existing cause. The fact that existence follows nonexistence belongs to what that existence is. What depends on the cause is existence itself, considered apart from what follows from it. The cause produces nothing but existence. Some existence is therefore called originated by its own nature, not because another cause or the thing itself made it so. Likewise, a body depends on a cause for its existence, but its boundedness follows from the body itself.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00753

An essence needs a cause for its existence because, by itself, it is equally open to existence and nonexistence; the cause gives it existence. But its being equally open to both, or the fact that its existence follows a prior absence—whether that absence is prior in nature or in time—is necessary and does not need a cause. The same holds for existence itself: it needs and is sustained by its cause because it is, by its own nature, weak, dependent, and like a shadow. What it receives from its cause is this dependent existence itself, not its being described as originated or eternal.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00754

Some later scholars put the point this way: for a reality that comes from another, dependence on that other is part of what it is, just as independence from all others is part of the Necessary Being’s reality. A dependent thing cannot remain the same dependent thing while becoming independent, just as what is independent of all things cannot become dependent. Either change would mean its nature had changed.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00755

Our view makes this especially clear. A thing that could exist or not exist depends on its maker because of its existence, not because of what the thing is. That very existence depends on its maker: the dependence is part of what makes it this existence. It cannot be thought of without that dependence; otherwise, it would no longer be this kind of existence. Likewise, existence that depends on nothing is what it is: if it became dependent, it would no longer be that. So dependent existence needs its cause at every moment, both when it begins and while it continues. Its need to continue is no different from its need to begin.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00756

This does not mean that the cause makes existence come after nonexistence, or after some earlier state. Those are features that follow from existence itself without being caused. What the cause makes is existence itself, not its features, including its not being eternal. God’s act is to give existence to things, sustain and preserve them, and keep each one for as long as its nature allows. Their defects and limits come from themselves.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00757

Here is an imperfect comparison. The sun shines freely on things that can receive its light. If something is kept in shadow, the obstacle is on its side, not the sun’s. Likewise, the One Being continually lights the forms of possible things and brings them from the darkness of nonexistence into the daylight of existence. If we imagine that He stopped giving them existence for even a moment, they would return to the darkness of their own nature. Glory to the Powerful, the Wise, who holds the heavens and earth so they do not fall; and if they were to fall, no one after Him could hold them.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00758

How mistaken are those who think the world needs its Sustainer only when it first comes into being, and not while it continues! Some have even said, out of ignorance and stubbornness, that if God’s nonexistence were possible, the world’s existence afterward would be unaffected, since He had already brought it into being. This is a deeply mistaken view. Every genuine cause exists together with its effect, both when the effect begins and for as long as it continues, as we will explain in our discussion of cause and effect.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00759

Fire gives heat to the bodies around it because heat belongs to its very nature, or form. Water makes nearby things wet because moisture belongs to it, just as heat belongs to fire. The sun lights the stars and bodies below because light belongs to its nature. What a thing does by its own nature does not change.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00760

Likewise, the soul gives life to the body. Life belongs to the soul’s nature and is a form that makes it what it is. The soul keeps giving life to the body, which is dead in itself but alive through the soul, as long as the body remains able to receive life from it. When the body loses this capacity, the soul leaves it. The same relation holds between every cause that produces its effect by its own nature.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00761

A builder puts together a house; a tailor joins pieces of cloth to make a garment. But treating this kind of assembly as a model of creation mistakes an indirect cause for a direct one. God does not merely join existing parts together, as some have claimed. He creates: He brings into existence what did not exist before. That is something different from assembling parts.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00762

Consider speech and writing. The speaker’s speech is like creation; the writer’s work is like putting parts together. When the speaker falls silent, the speech ends. When the writer stops, the writing remains. The world’s existence from God, exalted be His glory, is like speech from a speaker. All kinds of intellectual and soul existence, and all spiritual and bodily beings, are words of God that do not run out. If the sea of matter were ink for the words of existence spoken by its Lord, it would run dry before His words did, even if more seas were added from the matter of the heavens.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00763
This echoes the verse: “If every tree on earth were a pen, and the sea were supplied with seven more seas, God’s words would not run out. God is Mighty and Wise.”
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00764
XIV. A possible thing exists only if its cause makes it necessary
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00765

We have established that a possible thing does not exist unless something else tips the balance in favor of its existence. It does not cease to exist unless something else tips the balance towards its nonexistence. So whichever side is realized, the thing must have a cause outside itself that tips the balance.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00766

But how far must the cause tip the balance? Unless it makes one outcome necessary, it has not settled anything. Many theologians have thought that making existence preferable is enough, even if nonexistence remains possible. It is not. So long as either outcome can still occur, we must ask what makes one occur rather than the other. This supposed preference has left the choice between the two outcomes open. We would need another factor to settle it. If that factor also leaves both outcomes possible, we must look for yet another—and repeat the search without end.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00767

Even then, neither side has been settled. At every level, however many levels we suppose, the weak preference remains equally related to existence and nonexistence, even with all the assumed factors in place. So what we called the deciding cause has not decided anything. This shows that the assumption is impossible without appealing to the impossibility of an infinite chain of causes and effects; that question does not arise here. The contradiction is simpler: the factor assumed to decide the outcome does not do so. That would make the supposed deciding factor both a deciding factor and not one, which is impossible.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00768

In short, necessity is where the chain of possibilities ends. Actual existence is the starting point from which the many branches of unrealized powers unfold. That is why people say: necessity comes before possibility, actuality before potentiality, form before matter. Good prevails over evil, existence overcomes nonexistence, and God’s mercy comes before His anger, as we will explain in our discussion of potentiality and actuality.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00769

We have therefore shown that neither a thing that could exist or not exist, nor its dependent existence, becomes real unless its cause makes it necessary. A cause is not a cause of an effect unless it brings that effect about decisively. Once we speak of a cause and its effect, each necessarily stands in that relation to the other. The First Cause must not only exist; it must also be the source of other things. As we shall explain, God necessarily gives existence to what comes from Him. God willing, we shall return to this.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00770
XV. The two kinds of necessity and impossibility
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00771

The last chapter showed that, before either outcome occurs, a complete cause makes one of two things necessary: the thing will exist, or it will not. At the same time, that cause rules out the opposite outcome. Once either existence or nonexistence has actually occurred, a second kind of necessity applies. While a thing has a feature, it must be described as having it. So while a thing exists, it must be described as existing; it cannot at the same time be described as absent. And while it is absent, it cannot at the same time be described as present.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00772

Every possible thing—whether it exists or not, by itself or through another—is therefore subject to two kinds of necessity and two kinds of impossibility when we consider its cause and its actual state. In reality, it cannot be free of them, whether it exists or not. Yet what a thing is, considered by itself and apart from any cause or actual state, remains open to either existence or nonexistence.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00773

The earlier necessity and impossibility of a possible thing both come from something else. The same is true of the later necessity and impossibility if by “possible thing” we mean its essence. But if we mean the existence it has actually received, the later necessity and impossibility follow from existence itself.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00774

Here is why. When we say that an essence must exist at a certain time, we mean the essence under the condition that it exists. Existence is a condition for the statement, not a part of the essence. We do not mean that the essence and the idea of existence together form a new thing. The essence, considered under this condition, is already there; that is why the claim that it exists must be true. But the essence by itself remains possible, even though its actual existence is necessary in reality.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00775

The word “existent” also applies to every actual existence in a way that must be true for as long as that reality exists. If we imagine a particular dependent existence cut off from its cause, it has no reality at all. The essence, by contrast, remains possible in itself even when its existence comes from a cause.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00776

Every statement that describes something or connects it to a feature has this later necessity. It may also have another kind of necessity: the timeless necessity in “God exists and has power”; a necessity that depends on what the thing is; a necessity that depends on a description, whether the description is part of the thing or added to it; or simple possibility. In short, if existence or nonexistence applies to an essence at some time, the opposite remains possible when we consider the essence by itself. But if we consider the essence in the state it actually has, the opposite is impossible. This impossibility comes from that state or from the condition attached to it, not from the essence by itself. It is impossible through something else in one sense, and through the condition itself in another.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00777
1. A possible misunderstanding
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00778

Someone may think that a possible thing, taken together with its existence, cannot fail to exist by its own nature. After all, existence and nonexistence cannot be true at the same time. This would make existence necessary in itself, and the whole possible thing necessary in itself too.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00779

But this misses a point we have made several times: the necessity here is not timeless or absolute. It holds only while the thing remains in the stated condition. Someone who is human must be human while they are human. Likewise, a person who exists must exist while they exist. This necessity is really through another, because possible things exist—and are described as existing—only after a cause brings them into being. The same goes for a whole made from two things that are each necessary: the whole is necessary through another, not by itself. Likewise, a whole made from two impossible things is impossible through another. Before all its parts are together, the whole is not yet there; it becomes necessary or impossible only while it is a whole.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00780

Some have offered a poor escape from the argument. They say that an essence considered together with existence is only an idea in the mind, because they regard existence itself as an idea. How, then, could that imagined combination be necessary? But they have missed the point. No one is claiming that the idea alone must exist. We are speaking about what the idea refers to: the thing itself, considered while it exists. It necessarily exists in that condition, whether or not one accepts our view that existence is real outside the mind.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00781

Another respected scholar takes a different approach. He says that if nonexistence is impossible for a thing while it exists, then what must hold is only that the thing not be absent while it exists. This is a broader claim than saying that it exists at that time. It could still be true if the thing were absent at every time, because the condition “while it exists” would never arise. So, he concludes, the fact that a thing must exist while it exists comes from its cause and can be taken away from the essence itself.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00782

This argument would help only if necessity of existence followed merely from nonexistence being impossible. But our claim is that the essence, under the condition that it exists, must have existence—just as a part must belong to the whole and an effect must depend on its cause. A possible thing that exists must have existence, whether existence is its condition or part, or whether it depends on its cause or is produced by it. In the same way, a thing made by God cannot be separated from God while it is His creation: the cause is part of what sustains the effect’s existence. This is why the report has God say to Moses, “I am the one who stays close to you.” So we must return to the account we have established.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00783

One critic who tried to answer the defenders of truth with argument alone, and to imitate people of spiritual experience with words alone—like someone trying to fight a battle by carrying heavy gear—wrote in a book called The Incoherence of the Philosophers that the opposite side can be compared to a possible thing in several ways.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00784
First, we can compare it with the essence by itself, without considering what has actually happened to it. In that sense, the opposite side remains possible for it at that time and at every time.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00785

Second, we can compare it with the essence under the condition that the other side has occurred, without making that condition part of the essence. If we ask whether the opposite applies to the essence by itself, it may remain possible at every time, even though the actual condition makes it impossible at that time. If instead we ask whether the opposite applies to the essence as it is under that condition, the opposite may be possible in itself, may actually occur, or may be impossible in itself. For example, if we consider a possible thing as existing, its nonexistence may still be possible for its essence, even though it now exists. This does not mean it both exists and does not exist, because each claim concerns the essence in a different respect. But if we consider a possible thing as nonexistent, its existence is impossible for it in that respect.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00786

Third, we can compare the essence with its actual state as part of the thing we are describing. We can make the same two distinctions here. In this case there is even less reason to think that a contradiction follows. The critic concludes that the opposite is possible in itself in the first two ways of considering it, and impossible in itself in the last two.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00787

The weakness of this argument is clear if we remember what we have already explained. The question is not whether one side can be imagined as impossible in relation to the other, while the mind ignores what is real. The question is what the opposite side would be like in reality. An essence that actually exists cannot, in reality, fail to exist at that same time, whether we consider its state as a condition or as part of what we are describing.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00788

The subject of both claims is the same essence. We do not add the idea of “being under this condition” to the essence as if they formed a new thing in reality. We consider the real essence in a way that matches the mind’s description of it as existing. There is no real mixture in that essence—only a distinction the mind makes. So the opposite side is impossible for it in itself, and the side that actually holds is necessary in itself.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00789

This critic’s argument also fails when applied to existence itself. Existence is what makes something actually real, and in every case it comes with this later necessity. It is itself a real thing. In a statement such as “existence is real,” it is both the subject and what is said of the subject; its opposite, “existence is not real,” is impossible in itself. The only way through this difficulty is to keep apart the two kinds of necessity: the necessity that holds while a thing remains in a condition, which causes no problem, and absolute, timeless necessity, which does not follow here.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00790
2. Addendum
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00791

Any possible thing that has received existence and necessity through another at some time cannot fail to exist at that time. Nor can we say that it has no place anywhere in reality. That would mean it is absent from every level of reality, without restricting the claim to some other time. But we already know that it existed at one time.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00792

Thus, when we say that a thing which exists at one time could have been nonexistent, we mean that nonexistence is possible for its nature considered by itself. We do not mean that what actually existed has no place in reality.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00793
XVI. Why some possible things have one kind of possibility and others have two
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00794

Some possible things can receive existence from the generosity of the highest source simply because of what they are. They need no outside condition and no further feature to make them ready. Their existence therefore flows from the generous source without delay, without a stretch of time when they did not exist, and without any bodily preparation. Each has only one way of existing; its kind is represented by a single instance. Different instances of the same kind arise only when causes outside the essence make them different. What follows from a thing’s nature, or from a feature that belongs to it, does not change. So there is no room here for many different instances of the same kind.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00795

Other possible things cannot receive existence through their essence alone. Their nature gives them only the capacity to exist, not full readiness to receive existence. They need outside conditions and causes that do not belong to their essence. When the needed conditions come together in matter, the thing becomes ready to exist. What was once remote from its cause is now close enough to receive its action. Alongside the basic possibility of its nature, it has acquired a second kind of possibility: actual readiness. This readiness develops in changing matter over time, until the power to receive and the power to act meet. Through their coming together, something new is brought into existence.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00796

Every possible thing depends on a cause that must exist and is fully able to act. Such a cause cannot give existence to one thing that is ready and withhold it from another equally ready thing without a reason. Differences in what things receive must therefore arise from differences in their readiness.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00797

Anything that could exist has that possibility simply because of what it is. But suppose this alone were enough for God to bring it into existence. Since His giving is complete and holds nothing back, everything that could exist would exist immediately. Nothing would begin at one time rather than another. Yet we know that things do begin at different times.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00798

If basic possibility is not enough, and a thing needs further conditions before it can receive existence, then that thing has two kinds of possibility. The first is basic possibility: one general idea shared by every possible thing and belonging to its essence. The second is readiness, which appears when a thing’s basic possibility is not enough to receive existence. This second kind belongs to matter that exists before the thing in time and prepares it to pass from potential to actual. We have discussed this readiness before.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00799

With readiness, one essence can take on endlessly many forms. Matter can be prepared in endlessly many ways, and this receptive matter can meet a source whose power has no limit. So blessings continue to flow without end. If basic possibility were the only kind, the flow of existence would be blocked. Many possible things would remain forever in nonexistence, instead of becoming what they can be. We will prove later that this is impossible. Nothing in these claims conflicts with the sound teaching of religion or with sound philosophy.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00800

The mistake lies in saying that things that begin in time have always existed, or that the power of possibility has no limit. Events that follow one another in time come about only through motion, change, matter, and time. But things brought into being by direct creation are not always preceded by time and place. This is true whether they exist beyond time and place or are joined to them without undergoing gradual change. They are sources of motion, whether as things that move or as things toward which movement is directed.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00801

God is above all: the First, with nothing before Him; the Last, with nothing after Him. He is wholly active, with no potential waiting to be realized; wholly necessary, with no possibility of not existing; wholly good, with no evil; complete, with no lack; perfect, with no shortcoming; the goal of all things, with nothing left for Him to await; pure existence, with no essence apart from it.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00802

When two contrasting features are in question, what God directly gives is the nobler one. The other is not separately created; it follows from the limits of possible beings. Their existence is weak and mixed with the darkness of the nonexistence that comes with their limitations. The farther things are from the First Reality, the more their possibilities differ, and the more they vary in completeness, weakness, brightness, and obscurity.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00803

We have already said that necessity and possibility relate as completeness relates to lack. Anything that becomes necessary through another does so because of something that is not part of its essence. Burning, for example, is not necessary by itself. But when the active power of fire meets matter that can be burned, burning must occur. Think carefully: possibility and dependence come from distance from the source of necessity and independence. Actuality and existence come from nearness to that source. Possibility means separation and lack of connection, which lead to loss and disorder. Necessity means connection and union, which bring order. The more possibility there is, the more evil, loss, and disorder there are.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00804

When conditions remove some absences and block some obstacles to greater completeness, readiness appears. Readiness is a kind of perfection for something that is still only potential, considered as it exists in the outside world. Basic possibility, by contrast, belongs to an essence considered without existence at all. It is more hidden, darker, and more deficient than readiness, because readiness is actual in one respect even while the thing is still potential in another.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00805

A sperm, for example, is only potential to become a human being, but it already exists as a sperm. It is not yet a complete human, but it is fully what it is as a sperm. Basic possibility, by contrast, is only a lack of necessity: it has no actual side of its own. Readiness concerns a particular outcome, such as becoming human. Basic possibility concerns existence or nonexistence in general. The agent, not the essence’s own possibility, gives it a particular form. Readiness also disappears when the thing it prepares for comes about. Basic possibility remains when we consider the essence in itself, apart from its actual existence. It is not a stage that comes before existence in time. So a thing’s becoming actual and necessary in the outside world does not remove the basic possibility of its essence. That possibility belongs to the essence as such and cannot be removed by an outside cause. Readiness, which belongs to the actual world, does disappear when the thing is fully realized. Basic possibility therefore involves a deeper kind of need, weakness, and lack.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00806

Basic possibility is also the source of readiness. Matter, which makes room for loss and absence, comes from the active intellect through the possibility found in it. Since readiness has some existence, it can grow stronger or weaker according to how near the thing is to coming about. A sperm is less ready to become human than a clot of blood; the clot is less ready than a lump of flesh; and that is less ready than a complete body with the right organs, powers, and balance. Full readiness comes after basic possibility, when some causes have appeared and some obstacles have gone. It continues to grow until the thing comes about or opposing conditions arise.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00807

In short, the word “possibility” is used in two different senses. In one sense, one side is favored over the other. This kind can grow stronger or weaker, is not part of the possible thing’s essence, and belongs to something that already exists. It is an actual quality that prepares its subject to receive existence from the generous source. The new existence may arise directly in that subject, as a form or feature, or indirectly, as with a soul that does not depend on a body. The other sense of possibility differs from all this.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00808

When readiness is considered as belonging to the subject that has it, it is called that subject’s readiness. When considered in relation to the thing that will come about in it, it is called that thing’s possibility. This kind of possibility belongs to the thing that is ready, not to the future event as if it already existed. We describe the event as possible because its conditions are present in that thing.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00809

Some scholars say that readiness is simply the bodily quality itself, considered in relation to the form that will arise from it. The mixture in a sperm, considered by itself, is a bodily quality; considered in relation to the animal form that will arise, it is readiness. A courtyard is a feature of the house; when we consider how many people it can hold, we call that its capacity. We will return to the correct account in the chapter on potentiality and actuality, God willing.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00810
XVII. Some rules about what is impossible in itself
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00811

Just as the mind cannot grasp the reality of the Necessary Being in Himself—because He is so great, bright, complete, and beyond all limits—it cannot directly picture what is impossible in itself, taken precisely as impossible. Its whole nature is failure and nothingness. Just as the Necessary Sustainer cannot be contained by the mind because He encompasses everything, what is impossible in itself lies outside being and thinghood. It has no reality to point to, no content for the mind to contain, and no object for awareness or imagination to reach. We reach the judgment that something is impossible in itself through an argument about what follows from it, rather than by picturing it directly. In a different way, the proof of the Creator also proceeds through an explanation resembling a proof from cause to effect.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00812

A thing cannot be necessary both by itself and through another. Nor can it be impossible both by itself and through another. So anything that is necessary or impossible only through another is possible in itself. Anything that entails something impossible in itself is impossible in the respect in which it entails it, even if it may be possible in another respect. For example, giving a body infinite size entails the impossible claim that a bounded thing is unbounded. One side contradicts itself; the other is impossible because of that contradiction. So the body itself remains possible when we consider it apart from this impossible relation, just as an effect can be possible in itself but must exist because its cause exists.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00813

In short, when one thing’s existence necessarily entails another’s, there must be a cause-and-effect relation between them. The same is true when one thing entails another’s absence or impossibility: there must be some relation between them. Just as two Necessary Beings, if we imagined them, might coexist by chance without necessarily implying one another, two things that are each impossible in themselves do not form a strict logical link. Such a link is between something impossible in itself and something impossible through another; the latter is possible in itself. This also distinguishes a strict “if … then” statement from one based on coincidence. In a strict statement, the truth or falsity of the second claim follows from the truth or falsity of the first because of a necessary link between them. In a coincidental statement, there is no such link.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00814

In debate, people sometimes begin by assuming something impossible, hoping to show that another claim must be false. When challenged, they may reply: “Your assumption is impossible. Why could it not lead to the opposite conclusion? One impossibility can lead to another.” But that answer is wrong. An impossible claim does not imply just any other impossible claim. Even in a hypothetical case, the two must have a connection like that between cause and effect.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00815

A strict “if … then” statement joining two false claims may therefore be true or false. If the claims have a necessary connection—for example, a human being’s being a donkey and braying—the statement is true. If the claims rule one another out, the statement is false. If neither follows from nor conflicts with the other, we can only suppose that they might go together. We cannot prove it. Certainty requires a necessary connection; possibility alone gives us grounds only for conjecture.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00816
XVIII. How can we know what is impossible or nonexistent?
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00817

Whatever we know must be distinguishable from other things. And whatever can be distinguished must exist. It follows that anything we know exists, and that we cannot know what does not exist. Yet we do know that God has no partner and that contradicting claims cannot both be true. Neither of these supposed things can exist. How can we know them?
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00818

Something that does not exist may be simple or made up of parts. If it is simple—such as God’s having no opposite, partner, or equal—we understand it by comparing it with things that do exist. We can say, for example, that nothing stands to God as black stands to white. Nothing resembles Him, and nothing shares a kind or general class with Him. If we did not understand opposition, likeness, and shared kinds among existing things, we could not say that God has no opposite, likeness, or thing of the same kind, or anything else of this sort that cannot apply to Him.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00819

If the thing that does not exist is made up of parts, we understand it by knowing those parts. To know that opposites, such as black and white, cannot be together, we first understand black and white, then consider them together, where that is possible. We then say that although we can understand the idea of their being together, it does not occur in reality. This is the answer others have given: we understand the absence of something simple by comparing it with what exists, and the absence of something made up of parts by understanding its parts.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00820

My own answer is different. The mind can form an idea of anything, even what is impossible: absolute nonexistence, the absolutely unknown, two contradictions together, or a partner to God. The mind can make suitable claims about these concepts without saying that they exist outside the mind. As ideas, they have a kind of presence: we can call them things in a broad sense, say that they are possible to think about, or describe them as mental qualities, acts of knowledge, and the like. This gives us a basis for making claims about them.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00821

But when those same ideas stand for things that cannot exist, they give us no basis for making claims about such things as realities. If we distinguish the idea in our minds from what it supposedly stands for, we can say that nothing can be reported or affirmed of the nonexistent thing itself. This resolves the famous puzzle in the claim “Nothing can be said about the absolutely unknown.”
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00822

The key is that some concepts apply to themselves as ideas, but not as real things. The idea of “a partner to God” or “the absolutely unknown” is itself a concept, but it does not name an actual thing. In one sense, the concept applies to itself; in another, it does not. This is why we can correctly say that such a thing cannot exist.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00823
XIX. How one impossible thing can entail another
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00824

Remember that debaters often say an impossible assumption may lead to any impossible conclusion. That is not generally true. Two claims, whether possible or impossible, can be linked by necessity only if they have a connection of their own. In that case, once we grant one claim, the mind cannot separate it from the other. The connection may be between a cause and its effect, or between two effects of the same cause.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00825

A necessary link must be possible between the two things. So if two impossible claims could be linked, were they to occur, we may say that one entails the other. If there is no such link, we cannot. For example, if a whole made from two impossible things were to exist, then at least one of those things would have to exist. If Zayd were a donkey, he would bray. And a circular chain of causes would lead to an endless chain of causes. These are cases where one impossible claim entails another because of a necessary link.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00826

But two impossible claims may have no necessary connection. They may even conflict. A whole consisting of two things impossible in themselves could not exist if only one of those things existed. Likewise, if a human being were a donkey, that person could not at the same time be a horse that neighs. Nor could a donkey, under that very assumption, understand general ideas as a human intellect does. We can see some of these conflicts immediately; others require an argument.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00827
So the claim that one impossibility may imply another is true only in some cases. The claim that what actually occurs cannot imply an impossibility is true without exception.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00828

A strict “if … then” statement joining two false claims is true only if there is a necessary link between them. If they conflict, the statement is simply false. If there is no necessary link and no conflict, they may happen to go together, but we can accept that only as a possibility, not as a proven fact. Coincidence applies to things that actually exist; when both claims are false, their coincidence can only be supposed. We can be certain only when there is a necessary link. Mere possibility leaves room for doubt.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00829

Some people think that, for one impossible claim to possibly imply another, it is enough that the two do not conflict, even if there is no necessary link. Others require a necessary link. A third group thinks that two claims might necessarily imply one another even while they contradict each other. They try to allow both implication and conflict. But these cannot both be true in the same respect.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00830
Someone may also argue that a contradiction implies that both sides are absent, since each side rules out the other.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00831

The flaw is clear. If one side of a contradiction actually exists, then the other side is absent. But that is not the case we are considering. We are assuming the impossible situation in which both sides exist together. Under that assumption, the existence of one side implies the existence of the other, not that both are absent. So why would their being together imply that neither exists?
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00832

This also answers an objection about chains of strict “if … then” statements. Someone may say that the second link in such a chain can stop being true once the first claim is assumed. For example: “If this color were both black and white, it would be black. If it were black, it would not be white. So if this color were both black and white, it would not be white.”
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00833

The answer is that “black” does not mean the same thing in both statements. In the first, we are assuming that black and white can occur together. In the second, black means a colour that excludes white. Because the word changes its meaning, the two statements have no genuinely shared middle step. If “black” meant the same thing in both, the conclusion would follow. If it meant black as something that could occur alongside white in both, the second statement would be false.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00834

Avicenna raises a similar puzzle in The Healing: “If two were odd, it would still be a number. Whenever it is a number, it is even. So if two were odd, it would be even.” The answer is that if the second statement is only a coincidence, the chain proves nothing; a valid chain of positive “if … then” statements needs a strict link. If the second statement is strict, it is not true in every possible case in which two is a number. One such assumed case is that two is odd, and under that assumption it is not even.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00835

Someone may object that two cannot be odd while still being two, so evenness must follow whenever two is a number. Another answer is that “two is odd” is false in reality, but can be granted for the sake of argument. Anyone who grants it must also accept the conclusion within that argument; otherwise, they are no longer talking about the number two.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00836

Both answers make the same point. If being odd conflicts with being two in reality, that is no problem: a hypothetical case need not be possible in reality. But it is wrong to say the conflict holds under every assumption. We can suppose that two is odd, and under that supposition its being a number follows. So “two is even” does not follow from “two is a number” in every possible way the premise may be understood.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00837
XX. In what sense existence is added to a possible thing’s essence
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00838

Saying that existence is “added” to a possible thing’s essence does not mean that the two are separate realities. The reality of a thing is its own particular existence. Nor does it mean that existence is a separate feature attached to the essence, like a color attached to a body. That would mean the essence needs another existence beyond its own.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00839

What we call a possible thing’s existence is limited and dependent. Because of those limits, the mind can draw from it an idea distinct from existence itself: what the thing is. Think of the patterns cast by light as it grows weaker and gives way to shadow. The standard arguments for adding existence to what a thing is prove only that these are two different ideas. They do not prove that they are two separate realities.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00840

The first proof is that saying “a thing exists” tells us something, while saying “a thing is what it is” or naming its essential features tells us nothing new. Second, we may need an argument to establish that something exists—for example, an intellect that is not bodily. But we do not need an argument to show that a thing is what it is or has the features that make it that kind of thing. The third is that we can deny existence of an essence: “The phoenix does not exist.” But we cannot deny an essence or its essential features of themselves.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00841

The fourth proof is that existence has one shared meaning, while the essences of a human being, a horse, and a tree are different. The fifth is that we can think about what a thing is without deciding whether it exists in the outside world or in the mind. Someone might object: “But to think of something is for it to exist in the mind.” That has not been established. Even if an argument established it, thinking of something would not mean that we must also think about our thinking.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00842

Most people put the point this way: “We can understand an essence and still doubt whether it exists in reality or in the mind.” But this only shows that we can understand what something is without affirming that it exists. It does not prove that essence and existence are separate in reality. The reasoning shifts between what we understand and what we affirm, so it does not use the same middle term throughout.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00843

These five arguments, once fully stated, show only that the ideas of existence and essence are different. Yet what their proponents want to establish is that they differ in reality. Consider the divine attributes: for those who hold the truth, they differ in meaning but are one in reality, because the reality of God’s essence is itself the reality of all His perfect attributes, as we will see, God willing.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00844
XXI. How a possible thing’s existence is one with its essence outside the mind, and joined to it in a certain way
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00845

As we have shown, existence in its true sense—not the general idea of existence formed by the mind—is something real. If the existence of a possible thing were not one with its essence in reality, as a real thing is joined to an idea, then existence would have to be either the essence itself in meaning or one of its parts. Both possibilities have already been shown, by agreement and by reason, to be false. We can understand an essence without being aware of whether it exists, among other arguments already mentioned.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00846

Perhaps existence is something added to what a thing is, as whiteness is added to a body. But a quality can belong to something only if that thing already exists. Applied to existence itself, this would mean either that the thing exists before it exists, or that it has more than one existence in the same respect. Neither is possible. Something that has no existence of its own cannot carry a quality.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00847

If the essence were made existent by an existence added to it, the essence would have to exist before that existence, since what bears a quality must exist before the quality. The essence would therefore come before itself. If it existed through another existence, we would face the second problem: one essence would have multiple existences. This would lead to an endless chain of existences all present at once. Such a chain is impossible by proof, and would leave an infinite number of things between two limits: existence and essence. This, in turn, proves the point we seek: in reality, existence is the essence itself. For if every existence added to the essence depends on it, with none left out, then the essence must have an existence that is not added to it. Otherwise, the set would not be complete.
Stage One: Existence and its first divisions
passage-en-00848

Here is another argument. If existence were a quality present in an essence, then the essence bearing it would either be nonexistent, which is contradictory, or existent, which would lead to circularity or an endless regress. Someone might answer that existence belongs to the essence considered simply as it is—not to an essence that is nonexistent, which would be contradictory, nor to one that already exists, which would lead to circularity or an endless regress. But this reply does not solve the problem. Its defender compares existence with whiteness: whiteness, they say, does not belong to a body already white, for that would assume what we are trying to explain; nor does it belong to a body that is not white, for that would contradict the claim. It belongs to the body considered simply as a body.
